assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 3,000 business transactions/s at peak. 90% commit cleanly, 5% fail a step and run compensating actions, 5% are status polls from the caller. The 5% compensation rate is a payment-decline / out-of-stock rate, not an infrastructure failure rate.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: THE IMPORTANT CAVEAT: a saga is a SEQUENCE — commit, then compensate on failure — and the v1 engine is an open queueing network with no notion of ordering, in-flight state or elapsed saga lifetime. What is modelled is the steady-state per-second VISIT RATE each participant sees. It will size the fleet correctly and find the throughput bottleneck; it will NOT tell you the p99 end-to-end saga completion time, how many sagas are in flight, or what happens when a participant is down and retries pile up. Those need a discrete-event model.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Kafka capacity is stated in TRANSACTIONS/s, not messages/s. One saga costs roughly 7 broker messages (1 start + 3 commands + 3 replies); a broker sustaining ~20,000 msg/s therefore contributes ~2,800 transactions/s. The engine's visit_prob is a probability in [0,1] and cannot express a >1 visit ratio, so the fan-out lives in the capacity input instead of the flow.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The saga log is the durability anchor: every state transition is an fsync'd write, and the outbox is polled by the relay. Sized at ~4,000 rps on a single writer — the log is append-mostly but each write is synchronous. This component is the bottleneck at 3k tps and is the first thing to shard by saga id.

assumptions.subject: coord
assumptions.statement: Orchestration (not choreography): one coordinator owns the state machine. It is stateless between steps — all state lives in the saga log — so it scales horizontally, which is why 3 instances at ~1,500 rps each suffice.

assumptions.subject: pay
assumptions.statement: Payment authorisation is modelled at ~1,500 rps/instance with 12 ms of local service time. The remote card network / PSP round trip (typically 100-300 ms) is NOT included: an external rail has no per-instance capacity Keystone can size. Add it as a rate-limited external dependency before reading any end-to-end latency figure.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Idempotency keys are written before the first participant call and checked on every retry, which is what makes at-least-once delivery safe. The lock registry is advisory: it reduces conflicting sagas on the same entity, it does not guarantee isolation. Sagas are NOT serialisable — intermediate states are visible to other readers.

_library.summary: Orchestrated saga coordinator with a durable saga log, outbox relay and compensating transactions across order, inventory and payment services.
